speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: I welcome Members' comments or questions on both Bills after my speech.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: This allows the substantive points to be covered in a single debate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing) (for the Prime Minister)
text: We will still have the formal Second Reading of the Parliamentary Elections (Amendment) Bill later in adherence to procedural requirements.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The amendments can be grouped into five categories.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The first category seeks to improve voter access for overseas Singaporeans and Singaporeans residing in nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second category updates the election advertising laws to support informed voting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third category seeks to streamline the administration, as well as enhance accountability and transparency, of the election expenses regime.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The fourth category seeks to clarify and improve election processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The fifth category focuses on the amendments that apply specifically to streamlining administrative processes for Presidential Elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: General Election 2020, or GE 2020, held during the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighted two key issues in our electoral landscape.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In May and June last year, ELD sought feedback from various stakeholders, including political parties, nursing home operators and overseas Singaporeans, on special arrangements for voters residing at some nursing homes and postal voting for overseas Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Taking into account the feedback, clause 19 of the PEA Bill and clause 18 of the PrEA Bill empower the Returning Officer to make special polling arrangements in nursing homes, so that it is more convenient for voters who are in-patients or residents of nursing home to cast their votes there.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These include setting up a special polling station within the premises of the nursing homes, and deploying mobile polling teams to collect ballot papers from bedbound voters in the nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The selection of nursing homes for special polling arrangements would consider factors such as the number of voters in the nursing home and the practicality of deploying the mobile polling teams, taking into account the resources required.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The outcome of the pilot will help scope the provision of special polling arrangements at nursing homes for subsequent elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The list of nursing homes selected for the pilot will be made public on Nomination Day, if the election is contested.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Polling agents will be allowed to witness the conduct of polls at the nursing homes, to give candidates assurance on the integrity and secrecy of voting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While there were suggestions to introduce postal voting in the past, we have not implemented this given the challenges associated with postal voting which is, after all, a form of remote voting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members may ask if the Government has changed our position.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To be clear, the Government maintains the position that voting in-person at polling stations remains the most transparent and secure method of voting that best ensures that each person wanting to vote can be accurately identified as an eligible voter and only votes once.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, we recognise that it may not be possible, for various reasons, for overseas Singapore Citizens to travel to one of the overseas polling stations or to return to Singapore to vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With the introduction of postal voting, eligible Singapore citizens living, studying or working overseas will be able to mail in their votes even if there are travel disruptions or restrictions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As set out in clause 28 of the PEA Bill and clause 25 of the PrEA Bill, ELD intends to implement processes supported by technology to provide assurance on the integrity and secrecy of postal voting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members may also access the handout through the MP@SG Parl mobile app.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Step one is to register to vote overseas by applying online via ELD Voter Services.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: During registration, the overseas Singapore Citizen has to make a deliberate choice to either vote by post or at one of the overseas polling stations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Application to vote by post or at one of the overseas polling stations by an eligible overseas Singapore Citizen can be done anytime except during the period from the third day after the Writ of Election is issued until the end of the election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If he or she has chosen to vote by post, he or she will need to provide his or her wet-ink signature during the registration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Step two, an overseas Singapore Citizen who has opted to be a postal voter can log in to ELD Voter Services using his Singpass after Nomination Day to download and print his postal ballot paper and the prepaid return envelope.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Step three, the postal voter will mark his vote on the postal ballot paper, fold and insert it in the return envelope, and seal and sign on the return envelope.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Step four, the postal voter should then post the sealed return envelope without delay.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This has to be done during the postal voting period, which starts on the day immediately after Nomination Day and ends on the eve of Polling Day in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To ensure that only bona fide postal ballot papers are counted, there will be a pre-count process in Singapore to sieve out the return envelopes which do not meet the criteria for counting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The process is set out in the lower row of the handout on counting of postal votes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, the return envelope must bear the signature of the voter furnished during registration and an official QR code which is unique for each voter.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The QR code enables the wet-ink signature on the return envelope to be matched against the specimen signature furnished during registration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Candidates and counting agents will be able to observe this entire process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Next, let me touch on postal voting offences.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clauses 26 and 28 of the PEA Bill and clauses 25 and 26 of the PrEA Bill deal with offences pertaining to postal voting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These include forging or fraudulently defacing any return envelope, supplying any return envelope without due authority to any person, or unauthorised possession of a return envelope.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The present offences on improper handling of ballot papers will be extended to include postal ballot papers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These provisions seek to address the concerns surfaced during ELD’s engagements with political parties and overseas Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These amendments aim to support informed voting at elections, which is essential to Singapore's system of representative government.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Currently, the rules for online and non-online election advertising are set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 30 of the PEA Bill and clause 28 of the PrEA Bill elevate these provisions on online and non-online election advertising to the respective main Acts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These amendments are needed to enhance transparency, so that voters know who is communicating the election advertising, and accountability, by making persons publishing election advertising responsible for their communications.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The laws for OEA are largely unchanged by the Bills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The amendments are intended to provide greater clarity on the rules for online election campaigning and to address unique features and functionalities of online communication activities, especially since political discussions and campaigning are increasingly taking place online.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the same time, space is preserved for Singapore Citizens to participate in political discourse online.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, during the election period, barring Cooling-off Day and Polling Day, a Singapore Citizen can continue to publish OEA without adhering to published-by requirements, as long as the content is published in his individual capacity, he is not directed by others to do so and is not paid or did not pay to publish.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 2 of the PEA Bill and PrEA Bill each contains updated definitions on the scope of OEA.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, the meaning of publishing OEA is extended to include amplifying access, such as boosting, reposting, sharing or resharing of existing OEA.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Amplifying access increases the reach of the original content to more users and has a similar effect to publishing fresh content.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Hence, it should be held to the same requirements.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, OEA content is considered to be published in Singapore, if the content is accessible from Singapore, or if it originates in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To enhance transparency and accountability, clause 30 of the PEA Bill sets out the updated published-by requirements in a new section 61B.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For the PrEA Bill, this is in clause 28 and a new section 42B.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Currently, OEA is required to display the particulars of the person who is responsible for publishing the OEA, and the particulars of the person who directed the OEA to be published.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the OEA is paid for, it should also show the particulars of the person who paid for it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With the amendments, the particulars of the person who approved the content of the OEA must be shown as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the virtual world, it is easy to hide behind aliases and third parties to put out election advertising.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This amendment strengthens transparency, so that voters can better discern the persons responsible for the election advertising.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: From the start of the campaign period, election activity can only be conducted by political parties or candidates, or third party campaigners authorised by a candidate or their election agent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As paid election advertising constitutes election activity, clause 30 of the PEA Bill sets out the offence for unauthorised third parties to publish paid OEA.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The equivalent provision in the PrEA Bill is in clause 28.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The same clauses restate the ban on publishing or displaying election advertising on Cooling-off Day and Polling Day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These will replace current section 78B of the PEA and section 60A of the PrEA respectively.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In line with the updated scope of OEA, amplifying access to OEA which was published before the cooling-off period will also be subject to the ban to ensure space for voters to reflect on the issues at stake before casting their votes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The exceptions to the cooling-off period ban will be retained, including for private and domestic communications, such as individuals sharing election-related content within a private chat or closed group with family or a small group of friends.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Currently, the Returning Officer, or RO, has powers to issue directions to candidates or their election agents to address certain breaches of the OEA regulations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The RO can also specify that the corrective actions must be taken within a certain period of time, so that breaches are addressed promptly during the short campaigning period.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These powers are intended to address the concern that online content that breaches the elections laws can potentially spread rapidly and, hence, tip the playing field and impact electoral outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The RO will look at the specifics of each case, to determine the appropriate course of action.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If necessary, the RO can exercise these powers expeditiously, to uphold the integrity of our elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have witnessed how the threat of foreign interference in elections has intensified around the world, especially in the online space.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having OEA laws, and keeping them up-to-date, helps safeguard our electoral processes from external influence and ensure that Singapore’s future is only to be decided by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Besides having these laws, all political parties and candidates participating in elections have a vital role to abide by these rules to protect the integrity of our elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Now, let me elaborate on the amendments relating to non-online election advertising or “NOEA”.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 2 of both Bills defines NOEA which covers a wide range of non-online advertising, from electronic advertising by way of short messaging service or SMS, and telephone calls, to traditional advertising, such as a banner, flag or poster.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To maintain coherence in the treatment of OEA and NOEA, the published-by requirements continue to apply to NOEA.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The two new requirements will better enable voters to assess the credibility of the information presented when forming their views on their preferred candidate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 30 of the PEA Bill and clause 28 of the PrEA Bill stipulate that the public display of traditional election advertising should only commence during the campaign period under the authority of a permit granted by the RO, as per the current regulations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are exceptions, for example, flags that contain only the name and/or symbol of a political party, for the sole purpose of indicating that the office of the political party is located at or within a building.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 30 of the PEA Bill and clause 28 of the PrEA Bill also provide that the display of posters and banners must be at a place stated in a list of permissible locations in the regulations, and not within the 50-metre zone around any polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, posters and banners may be hung on street lamp posts along public roads outside the 50-metre zone around any polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These amendments serve to strengthen the well-established principle that Singapore politics are for Singaporeans alone to decide.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To facilitate public inspection of election expenses returns, clause 36 of both Bills will allow for the publication of all election expenses online for greater transparency.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This will allow voters and other stakeholders to inspect the returns filed by candidates free of charge without having to make a trip to ELD.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To further enhance the accountability and transparency of our election processes, clause 37 of the PEA Bill provides powers to the RO to audit any election expenses returns submitted for parliamentary elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Allowing the election authorities to audit a candidate’s election expenses returns is not a new concept.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Countries, such as Canada, New Zealand and the United Kingdom, require some form of audited election expenses returns from the candidates or from the political party that fielded the candidates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Under the current law, a polling station for an electoral division can only be situated within the electoral division boundary.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Currently, to ensure that children are protected from exploitation during elections, a person attending a primary or secondary school as a student is prohibited from taking part in election activities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To ensure that Singapore politics is only for Singaporeans to decide, foreign individuals and foreign entities should not be allowed to participate in election activities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The current PEA and PrEA prohibit foreign individuals from participating in election activities but are silent on foreign entities, such as foreign companies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I will now cover the amendments relating to events that disrupt the election process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Currently, the provisions to deal with disruptive events are in the PEA and PrEA, which mean that any amendment that needs to be made to respond to contingencies will need to be passed in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: From the experience of the COVID-19 pandemic, there is a real need to provide greater flexibility in addressing disruptive events, to enable contingency arrangements to be put in place quickly, should they be required, to enable an election to be conducted while meeting the needs of the situation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 44 of the PEA Bill and clause 43 of the PrEA Bill allow the Minister to make regulations so that contingency arrangements can be put in place in a more timely and effective manner.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The definition of disruptive events is also expanded to include transport accident, unplanned or prolonged outage of any telecommunication or electricity service, or an information and communications system, which is essential for the proper conduct of an election.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Any regulation made under the Act to implement such contingency arrangements must be presented to Parliament as soon as possible after publication in the Government Gazette.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These amendments are administrative in nature to streamline the presidential election processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, the Presidential Elections Committee, or “PEC” in short, is responsible for ensuring that candidates for the office of the President have the required qualifications prescribed in the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, the applicant must be a person of integrity, good character and reputation and has met either the public or private sector service requirement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 3 of the PrEA Bill streamlines the processes to remove the requirement for the PEC to consider applications from applicants who do not meet the minimum age of 45 years on Nomination Day to qualify as a Presidential candidate.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Clause 4 of the PrEA Bill allows the PEC to reject an application from an applicant who does not state in his community declaration that he considers himself to be a member of the community that the election is reserved for.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The next amendment relates to the Community Committee, or “CC” in short.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The function of the CC is to decide whether a person who has submitted a community declaration belongs to the Chinese community, the Malay community or the Indian or other minority communities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Currently, the CC is required to notify every declarant that their community declarations have been accepted for consideration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With the proposed amendments under clauses 5 and 6 of the PrEA Bill, the CC will only be required to notify declarants in the following cases.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, to notify a declarant in an open election, who had declared that he did not belong to any of the prescribed communities, that his declaration has been accepted.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, to notify a declarant that his community declaration has been rejected as it is incomplete, or, in the case of a reserved election, not made for the relevant community the election is reserved for.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In all other situations, the community declaration will be accepted for consideration without the need for explicit notification.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I will cover three aspects: first, enabling more Singaporeans to vote; second, on the counting of votes; and third, on election advertising.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My party colleague Gerald Giam will speak later on voting by persons with disability and seek some other clarifications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers’ Party is in support of enabling more Singaporeans to exercise their right to vote at national elections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In principle, we welcome the changes to enable more Singaporeans overseas and those in nursing homes to cast their votes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as overseas voters are concerned, the Workers’ Party supports the implementation of postal voting to enable more Singaporeans abroad to vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The current scheme of requiring overseas voters to physically turn up at only 10 polling stations in six countries severely limits the ability of overseas Singaporeans to vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the Bill, overseas Singaporeans can vote from presumably any country with postal connections with Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It has the potential of empowering many more overseas Singaporeans to have their say in our national elections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as nursing homes are concerned, this will enable those who need residential nursing care to participate in elections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Bill provides for special polling stations and for mobile teams to be deployed at nursing home premises to facilitate this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is envisaged that the mobile teams may issue and collect ballot papers “by the bed”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that this is implemented elsewhere, such as in the United States.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have a few clarifications concerning the proposed arrangements at nursing homes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the proposed section 47A, the Returning Officer (RO) will decide whether to include a particular nursing home for special polling arrangements, depending on the likelihood of “a significant number of electors” who are residing there and who are unable to travel out to the ordinary polling stations, but are able to vote within the nursing home.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My question here is how will ELD determine whether voters in the nursing homes have the necessary mental capacity to cast their votes?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will ELD, for example, start gathering data from these nursing homes well ahead of the elections, including categorising the residents to determine who are mentally well enough to exercise their vote independently?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will the nursing home pre-screen those who have dementia or Alzheimer’s, or will it be left to the mobile teams to do this assessment at the point of voting?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is a need for assurance to nursing home residents that their vote is secret and should be freely exercised.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is particularly important as, unlike other seniors, residents of nursing homes are more frail and dependent on the care they receive, often at subsidised rates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Some residents may worry about the consequences of their vote.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These fears may be irrational, but I believe assurances to them about the secrecy and freeness of their vote are critical.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What measures will be taken in this regard?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On a related note, it is stated by the proposed section 47A(4) that voting at such special polling stations should be conducted, as far as possible, in the same manner as that in an ordinary polling station.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note, for instance, that at an ordinary polling station, there is some randomness in the allocation of the ballot paper, and also privacy at the time the vote is marked and cast.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will this be assured at the nursing homes, especially when mobile teams go to the voters’ bedsides?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would also like the Minister’s confirmation that polling agents from political parties will be admitted to these nursing homes to safeguard the voting process, similar to ordinary polling stations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 21 expands the methods of vote counting.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The proposed section 49(4A) states that counting may be done manually or by mechanical or electronic means.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 2 will define electronic means as using an electronic service, and electronic service is, in turn, defined to mean services that allow end-users to access content or receive content, including a social media service.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In ELD’s media release on this Bill issued on 6 February 2023, there is nothing mentioned about this change at all.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is some concern that the use of online services to count votes potentially exposes the vote counting process to hacking and glitches.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the Explanatory Statement to the Bill, the intention of clause 21 is to simply enable the use of counting machines as part of the counting process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During the last General Election in 2020, standalone machines were used for vote counting.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At that time, ELD was at pains to emphasise that the counting machines were not connected to the Internet and that there were also other safeguards, such as repeating the counting process using different machines.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will counting agents be able to audit the counting process?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I move on to the amendments relating to Election Advertising.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To appreciate what these new requirements will entail, I will refer to the examples given in the Explanatory Statement to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, for printed handbills containing a slogan, candidates and parties will be further required to include the identity particulars of the election agent of the candidate and the candidate’s senior campaign staff who approved the content of the slogan.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In another example, if a party engages a marketing firm to run its election campaign, the identity of the marketing firm will have to be stated in various situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the case of campaign staff working on campaign slogans, it is useful to take a typical scenario for clarification.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If staff brainstorm on a slogan, and the final approval of the slogan is given by the candidate or the party, I would assume that there would be no need to name the staff involved.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After all, campaign staff helping political parties ultimately take instructions from the party leadership.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for marketing firms, they are commercial entities who take on briefs for reward.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such firms can have multiple clients from different political parties over time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They are responsible for the content put out, and will be held liable for its contents.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is stated in the Explanatory Statement to the Bill that there will be a “positive list of permissible locations”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister clarify what practical difference this will make, compared to past elections?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What assurance will candidates and parties have that there will be adequate space in prime locations for all participants?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Looking at the Bill, these changes to election advertising are very detailed and must have been under consideration for quite some time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet, the changes were announced just a month ago, just before the Budget Statement and the Committee of Supply debates, which just concluded a few moments ago after 70 hours.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The timing of the Second Reading debate on this important Bill may account for the few speakers we see listed today, just two of us from the Workers’ Party and, of course, Member Louis Ng.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, I would like further elaboration on the changes to the counting of votes and election advertising requirements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Workers’ Party maintains its position on being opposed to the office of the Elected President.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The reasons for this position have been canvassed over the decades since the 1980s, and I do not intend to repeat them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As such, we are not speaking on that Bill, and will vote to abstain then.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In my speech today, I would like to make a proposal that could help PwDs more fully participate in the election process.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: According to the Government, the election official is obliged to mark the ballot paper in the manner directed by the voter and is under oath to keep the vote secret.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has the Government considered the possibility that some PwDs would prefer to have someone they know and trust to help them to vote?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is a concern also expressed by the Disabled People’s Association (DPA).

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Other countries, such as Canada and Germany, allow friends and family to assist a PwD with voting.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Incorporating this measure will better ensure that PwDs can exercise their right to vote in a smooth and comfortable manner, while upholding the secrecy of their vote and election integrity.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, the Bill allows for votes to be counted by electronic means.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This adds to previous amendments to the Act where electronic voting was permitted.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When votes are counted by manual or mechanical means, counting agents appointed by the candidates and the candidates themselves are able to personally witness the counting of all the votes.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They can physically ensure there is no mis-count of votes for each candidate.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister clarify how the candidates and their counting agents will be able to audit the votes counted by electronic means?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The rest of the questions in this speech relate to this period.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Parliament is dissolved when the Writ of Election is issued.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: When this happens, every Member of Parliament ceases to be a Member of Parliament, according to Article 46(1) of the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore, and their allowances cease to be paid.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: After Parliament is dissolved, are the former Members of Parliament allowed to hold Meet-the-People sessions (MPS) in their constituencies, interact with residents and provide assistance to them?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Can they write appeal letters to Government agencies or other organisations on behalf of their constituents and, if they do, are agencies obliged to respond to them?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: It should be noted that many residents will not be aware that Members of Parliament stand down after Parliament is dissolved and will continue contacting their Members of Parliament for assistance, sometimes on urgent personal matters or municipal matters that have safety implications.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Next, do grassroots adviser (GRA) appointments cease when the Writ is issued?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If not, can GRAs continue operating as per normal after the Writ is issued, including writing appeal letters to Government agencies on behalf of residents?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is "campaigning" allowed from the day the Writ is issued to Nomination Day?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are potential candidates allowed to conduct house-to-house visits or visit markets and coffee shops, to either check on residents’ well-being or explicitly canvass for votes, while wearing their party uniforms and badges?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Just before previous elections, some incumbent Members of Parliament and potential candidates conducted some of these activities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, a Yahoo News article entitled "GE2020: Josephine Teo to leave Bishan-Toa Payoh GRC to contest in Jalan Besar" reported that Mrs Teo was “seen during a People's Action Party (PAP) walkabout at Beo Crescent on Monday morning (29 June), together with Jalan Besar incumbent Members of Parliament Denise Phua and Heng Chee How, as well as new candidate Wan Rizal Wan Zakariah.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They were introduced to the residents as candidates contesting the GRC.” That year, Parliament was dissolved on 23 June and Nomination Day was 30 June.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This constituency walkabout took place within that period.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In another article in The Straits Times, it was reported that the then-National Development Minister Lawrence Wong announced the PAP’s slate in Marsiling-Yew Tee GRC at a walkabout in the Marsiling ward of the GRC on 28 June – again, within this period.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There was even a video of the team, consisting of Mr Lawrence Wong, Mr Zaqy Mohamad, Mr Alex Yam and Ms Hany Soh, together with Mr Ong Teng Koon, the former MP of the ward, at a coffee shop wearing their PAP all-white uniforms.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: At least two members of the group were wearing a PAP badge.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to the Minister's addressing the questions and concerns I have raised.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am, of course, glad to speak and I have clarifications in three areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first area of clarification relates to election advertising requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: First, the definition of "publish" will be amended to include forwarding and sharing content.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Given the ease of forwarding and sharing content on the Internet, it is not difficult to fall foul of these provisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A number of provisions provides that the prosecution does not have to prove that an accused knew or had reason to believe that the content includes election advertising.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is a general defence for the accused to prove that he or she did not and could not reasonably have known of the offence and took all reasonable steps and exercised all due diligence.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If interpreted strictly, this defence can be difficult to establish.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Specific to election advertising, can Minister clarify whether it will be a defence for the accused to prove that he or she did not, in fact, know that the content includes election advertising?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, since the meaning of "content" includes hyperlinks and items that store data electronically, would it be a defence for the accused to prove that he or she did not access the hyperlink or folder?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the public should, of course, responsibly share information online, there is also a difference in culpability between a layperson who carelessly forwards messages and links to a friend and a political operator looking to influence the elections.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share how the enforcement of the provisions relating to publication of election advertising will take into account the differences between these two scenarios?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Second, the Bill states that election advertising must include the identity particulars of persons who authorised making available to the general public the advertisement and who directed the election advertisement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister provide some examples to clarify the difference between authorising and directing an election advertisement?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Third, "publish" will exclude any communication of content between two or more individuals that is of a private or domestic nature by electronic means.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify what private or domestic means given that a chat on WhatsApp and Telegram can range from two participants to thousands?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, can Minister clarify how publication provisions will apply to a situation where communication of content between two or more individuals that is initially private or domestic in nature is subsequently forwarded on a wider scale?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second area of clarification relates to the penalties for breach of election advertising requirements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But the failure to include required information in election advertising may be caused by honest mistakes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such offenders are clearly less culpable than offenders who deliberately withhold information or provide false information.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share if individuals will be given an opportunity to correct breaches of election advertising requirements?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third and last area of clarification relates to the special polling arrangements at nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The amendments will allow special polling arrangements and mobile polling to be arranged to facilitate voting at nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A person in charge of a nursing home may inform the mobile polling team that a visit to an in-patient or resident is forbidden on medical grounds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The mobile polling team is then not allowed to visit or take the individual's vote.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share what safeguards are in place to ensure that the person in charge exercises such powers responsibly?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For instance, will a doctor's report be required to substantiate the medical grounds for forbidding the visit by a mobile polling team?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the wishes of the resident to vote be taken into account?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: More generally, the Returning Officer is required to consider the conditions of electors, practicality and other peculiar circumstances in deciding whether to set up special polling stations and mobile polling teams.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are highly fact specific questions that require an understanding of the residents and healthcare knowledge.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2021, there were about 80 public, private and not-for-profit nursing homes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister share how the Returning Officer will make an informed assessment individually specific to all nursing homes?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Returning Officer be required to seek the advice of medical and geriatric healthcare professionals in ensuring that any polling arrangements are appropriately made?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Louis Ng and Ms Sylvia Lim sought clarifications on the amendments pertaining to election advertising.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There is also a defence for persons who breached election advertising rules due to circumstances beyond their control, for example, if the breach was due to sabotage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ultimately, any defence has to be considered based on the facts of each case.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Louis Ng also asked for clarifications on the difference between authorising and directing an election advertisement and Ms Sylvia Lim asked for the rationale for naming the individuals and entities who approved the content of the election advertisement, even though they ultimately take instructions from the candidates or political parties.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The published-by requirements require that election advertising displays the full names of all persons who played an active role in publishing it.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Such persons include: one, the person who authorised making available to the general public the election advertising; two, he person who approved the content in the election advertising; and three, the person for whom or at whose direction the election advertising was published.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For any election advertising, these three persons may or may not be same.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: A political party hires a social media influencer for a fee, to post election advertising on social media on its candidate's behalf.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As required under the law, the candidate must first provide written authorisation to the influencer to conduct election activity on his or her behalf.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Thereafter, the candidate approves the content prepared by the influencer, before the influencer publishes the content on his or her social media account.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In this case, the political party is deemed to have directed the influencer to publish the election advertising, while the candidate had approved the contents of the election advertising.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Meanwhile, the influencer is deemed to have authorised the publishing of the election advertising, since the election advertising was published on his or her social media account.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Hence, the full names of the political party, the candidate and the influencer must be displayed on the social media post.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The post should also state that it was paid for by the political party.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Louis Ng also had a question on the meaning of private or domestic communication.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As stated in my opening speech, examples of private or domestic communication include sending or forwarding election-related content within a private chat, or a closed group with family or a small group of friends.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When deciding whether a communication is of a private or domestic nature, the Returning Officer, or RO, will make a case-by-case assessment, taking into consideration three factors: first, the number of individuals in Singapore who are able to access the content; second, whether there are restrictions to access the content, including whether it is a public or closed group; and third, the relationship between the sender and receiver of the content, for example, whether they are strangers or known to each other.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Next, Mr Louis Ng sought clarification relating to the penalties imposed for breaching the new election advertising requirements, whether individuals will be given an opportunity to rectify breaches of election advertising requirements and whether the penalties for such breaches are too "harsh" since if convicted, a voter may be banned from voting for seven years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These requirements are there to promote informed voting and to safeguard our elections from external influence.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The penalty for not complying with these requirements is thus serious.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Further enforcement action will be considered only if the individuals do not comply.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Giam asked about the kind of election activities allowed in the period from the day the Writ of Election is issued to Nomination Day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Political parties and candidates may continue to conduct routine activities, as long as they are conducted within the limits of the law.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On Mr Gerald Giam’s other requests on whether former Members of Parliament are allowed to hold Meet-the-People Sessions to interact with residents, provide assistance to them, whether grassroots advisors can continue to operate as per normal after the Writ is issued, and the Candidate Handbook, these questions are out of the scope of the Bills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Gerlad Giam may wish to file Parliamentary Questions and we will be happy to answer them separately.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Lim asked about the amendment to require the display of posters and banners only in permissible locations and whether all political contestants will be assured of ample space in prime locations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I am sure that will be sufficient space for all political parties to do the necessary.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Louis Ng noted that a person in charge of a nursing home may inform the mobile polling team that a visit to a resident or in-patient is forbidden on medical grounds, and asked about the safeguards in place to ensure that this is not abused.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is to safeguard their well-being and safety.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On Ms Sylvia Lim’s question on voters with some limitation in mental capacity, we will adopt the same approach as that for regular polling stations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is, before the issuance of ballot paper, the election official will request the voter for his identification document and poll card.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the voter does not respond to the election official’s request for his identification document and poll card after a few attempts, the voter will not be issued a ballot paper.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would also like to assure Ms Sylvia Lim that for those who are able to make their way to the special polling stations set up at the premises of the nursing homes, the procedures are the same as the regular polling stations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Candidates will be able to send polling agents to the nursing homes to observe that voting continues to be secret and that the various procedures are adhered to.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked whether a voter with disability can request someone who is known and trusted by him to help him vote.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Over the years, ELD has introduced various initiatives to make it easier for them to do so, such as stencils for those who are visually impaired and lap booths for those on wheelchair.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If the voter is physically unable to mark the ballot paper, he can request for an election official to assist him.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These arrangements have served us well and we have no plans to change them currently.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As Mr Ng rightly noted, the Bill sets out various factors that the RO is required to consider.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In preparation for the roll-out of this new voting arrangements at these nursing homes, ELD has engaged MOH to understand the profiles of the residents and in-patients.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: ELD also visited these nursing homes to understand their unique context and environment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While ELD does not rule out any future solutions that can help enhance our election processes, electronic voting currently requires information on the voter's vote to be retained in the system for audit purpose.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This makes it challenging to maintain voting secrecy in the event that an audit has to be done.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would also like to assure Ms Lim that ELD will consult the political parties as it has done in the past, should advancement in technology allow the safe and secure use of electronic voting machines before rolling this out.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Giam may also wish to note that the section 50B of the Parliamentary Elections Act currently sets out the various requirements to be fulfilled before electronic counting machines can be used.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This includes testing of the system in the presence of candidates and their agents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: ELD has consulted political parties on the key initiatives on the new voting modalities last year in 2022 and these are part of the continuous efforts of ELD to enhance our electoral processes and election administration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Lim asked if we are going to pre-screen the electoral roll before we determine the nursing homes to be involved.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As for how many people will be eligible to vote in a nursing home, this will depend on those people who have previously registered.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we do not pre-screen as a procedure, those people that pre-register.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But as I explained, during the voting, the election officials will make that assessment as to whether the person has the mental capacity to conduct the voting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We agree with Members that the secrecy and the neutrality of the elections officials are very important.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is why the current mode is for the election officials to conduct this rather than to certify many other individuals who are not election officials to help respective individuals.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ms Lim can also be assured that the randomness of the issuance of ballot paper is the same as any polling station.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: You asked whether polling agents can assess, I think I have answered that, answer is yes, to view the processes in the nursing home.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And electronic means, we have answered that as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The counting machines are not connected to the Internet.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Mr Gerald Giam asked about whether we can qualify individuals to help the PwDs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As I have explained, I think it is best that we do this in a way that gives us confidence that the officials are cleared, neutral, impartial in their work rather than to clear many individuals for respective needs which we may not have the confidence to say that they are all clear about the processes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: With that Mr Speaker, Sir, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I urge all Members on both sides of the house to give your fullest support to both Bills.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Speaker, I have got two clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First is that, is it the intention that Minister will actually issue subsidiary legislation well ahead of the election to cover as many scenarios as possible?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And during the election, he alluded to the fact that there may be a need to issue some further regulations, for example, a transport incident – that was what he mentioned.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Does he foresee that since the Minister will be a participant in the election itself, that there will be any issue with the issuance of those sorts of regulations?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, that is the first thing about the regulations concerning disruptive events, that most of them will be issued well ahead of election, and during the election, it would be limited to extreme exigencies; and whether there is any issue with the Minister being a participant in the election, issuing those regulations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: And lastly, just a clarification on nursing home voting.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Will the ELD be conducting special voter education at the nursing homes to be chosen for the pilot, for the reasons which I mentioned earlier?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The quick answer to the first one is, yes, of course, the Minister will work with ELD to try to anticipate all the possible contingencies that we have to deal with prior to the elections.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I am sure you agree with me that during the election period, you are as busy as me.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Not the time for us to make new regulations at that point in time.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I believe he said just now that section 50B of the PEA allows for the inspection and testing of voting machines and vote counting machines.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: I cannot remember the exact words that he used.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: However, I believe that section 50b(2) actually requires for the inspection and testing of DRE voting machines and direct recording electronic voting equipment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: But it does not mention vote counting machines.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: So, can I confirm that vote counting machines will be included in this pre-election audit by the candidates and their polling agents?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That was demonstrated to all the political parties prior to ensure that the accuracy of the system.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, would you like to abstain for this Bill?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Would you like to record your dissention by standing in place, please?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Technically, you should have stood up before I say "the ayes have it".

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Perhaps you might want to raise your dissension later, at the Third Reading instead?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: When I declared that "the ayes have it, the ayes have it", that has passed, process wise.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The question is, "That the Bill be now read a Third time." As many of the opinion say aye, to the contrary say no.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Speaker, we request our abstention to be recorded.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: For those who want to record your dissention, please stand in place.
